one_liner: Research scripting language and VM in C (RTL bytecode, type-inferred specialization, GCC-based JIT); beats Python 3.4 and Ruby 2.1 interpreters.
what_it_does: Dino is a dynamically typed, C-like scripting language by GCC developer Vladimir Makarov, with its own bytecode compiler and interpreter. It offers extensible arrays and slices, hash tables, closures, classes composed through `use`, fibers (green threads), exceptions, pattern matching, multi-precision integers and a C FFI. It is a separate language with its own `dino` executable, not a faster runtime for Python or Ruby code. Its main value to a C/C++ engineer is as a readable reference design for a fast interpreter, documented in the README slides and an accompanying preprint.
how_it_is_fast: Bytecode is register-based with multi-operand instructions (RTL) rather than a stack machine. Instruction combining fuses common sequences: add, compare and branch becomes a single `btltinc`. With `-O`, a whole-program type inference pass builds a CFG, def-use chains and forward data-flow, then specializes generic instructions into typed ones (add into iadd or fadd) that skip operand type checks. Optional per-function hints add inlining (`!inline`), result caching for pure functions (`!pure`), and a function-level JIT (`!jit`) that turns bytecode into C and compiles it with GCC on first call. In the preprint's ablation on a six-deep nested loop (i7-4790K), CPU time drops from 6.51 s for a stack VM to 2.12 s with RTL, 1.38 s with combining, 0.61 s with JIT and 0.14 s with type inference and specialization. Memory management combines mark-and-sweep with a mark-and-copy collector and uses simple escape analysis to move heap allocations onto the stack.
when_to_use: Studying or porting interpreter techniques into your own VM (RTL bytecode, superinstructions, type-inference-driven specialization, a JIT that emits C for GCC); the preprint's ablation table shows what each step bought.
Integer loop and array-heavy scripts: on x86-64, plain Dino without hints was 13.5x faster than Python 3.4 on an empty loop and 37.9x faster on sieve (derived from page data).
Producer-consumer concurrency on one core: green-thread fibers took 1/125 of Python's time and 1/43.6 of Ruby's on the thread benchmark.

Tools that start the interpreter often or load huge generated scripts: startup was 10.9x faster than Python and 29.4x faster than Ruby, and compiling a very long assignment list was 3.3x faster than Python.
when_not_to_use: Production use: development stopped in 2019, there is no release after the 0.98 development snapshot (issue #21, 'When release a new version?', is open), and build issues remain open (#13 ONIGURUMA/missing, #12 -liconv on Darwin).
Object-heavy or call-heavy code against a tracing JIT: PyPy 2.2 beat plain Dino on 8 of 14 x86-64 benchmarks (method 0.2, object 0.1, fact 0.4 relative to Dino's best run).
Code that needs the Python or Ruby ecosystem; Dino is its own language with a small standard library.
Proprietary embedding: the interpreter is GPL-2.0-or-later (only the AMMUNITION support library is LGPL), and an embedding API is not documented.
Multi-core parallelism: fibers are green threads; OS threads without a GIL are listed only as a plan.

integration.form: built interpreter (autotools configure and make, plus `make install`); C functions plug in as shared objects (-L option) or as inline `%{ %}` C blocks compiled at run time
integration.dependencies: GMP; bundled Oniguruma 6.0.0 regexp library and the COCOM tools (SPRUT, MSTA, SHILKA, AMMUNITION) in the same repo; a C compiler (GCC) at run time for `!jit` functions and inline C
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; configure targets GCC (adds -Ofast, or -O3 as a fallback, plus -flto when supported); the preprint used GCC 4.9.2 for JIT compilation on Fedora Core 21
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows via Cygwin, macOS (Xcode and GMP needed); benchmarked on x86-64, AArch64, 32-bit ARM and PPC64
integration.thread_safety: Fibers are green threads scheduled by the interpreter; simple statements are atomic and there is a `wait (cond)` statement; no OS-thread parallelism.

gotchas: Harness flaw in the README tables: the 'Dino best = 1.0' row for fact and fib uses the `!pure` hint, which caches arguments and results of pure-function calls (preprint section 3.3.2; the manual defines the hint). fact(12) repeated N times and naive fib then become cache lookups, while Python, Ruby and PyPy run the full recursion. Only the plain Dino row is like-for-like, and its ratios have to be divided out: Python vs plain Dino on fib is 492/112 = 4.4x, not 492x (derived from page data).

DINO/compare.tst times each variant once with `time -p` and records user CPU time only. System time is ignored, helper threads in other runtimes add to their user time, and Dino's base is the minimum over plain, `-O` and hinted variants. Which of plain or `-O` produced the README's plain Dino row is not stated.

Default GCC builds use -Ofast (which implies -ffast-math) plus -flto (DINO/configure.ac), so the interpreter's own float arithmetic is not guaranteed IEEE-strict; the compiler version behind the 2016 tables is not stated.

`!jit` invokes a C compiler on a function's first call (the README says 50-70 ms for a small function) and writes temporary C and object files (to /tmp per the manual), so short scripts pay that cost and target machines need GCC installed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For an embeddable, permissively licensed fast interpreter, choose Wren (MIT; it beats Lua 5.2, Python 3.3 and Ruby 2.0 on its own suite) or LuaJIT. For raw speed on dynamic code, choose PyPy, which beats plain Dino on most object and call benchmarks. Pick Dino only as a reference implementation of RTL bytecode plus type-inferred specialization and a GCC-emitting JIT, or if you specifically want its language features.
verified_claims_summary: First-party April 2016 README tables (Dino 0.98 dev; x86-64 i5-4670 Haswell, plus X-Gene, Exynos 5410 and Power7) give user CPU times relative to Dino's best variant, on old shootout-style programs run by DINO/compare.tst. Plain Dino without hints beat Python 3.4.x by 13.5x on loop, 6.8x on fact, 4.4x on fib and 37.9x on sieve, and Ruby 2.1.x by 8.3x, 1.9x, 1.3x and 4.5x (derived from page data). PyPy 2.2 was faster than plain Dino on 8 of 14 x86-64 benchmarks.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-11-19 (129 stars, 10 open issues including build failures) and GPL-2.0-or-later. Useful as readable reference code for interpreter design rather than as a dependency.
